title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated video and fabricated social media profiles were used to make scammers appear to be a real, named attorney. The failure did not occur inside a legitimate AI deployment. It occurred in the deliberate misuse of AI tools to produce synthetic content at scale, with hundreds of fake profiles and videos created across multiple platforms before any platform-level detection removed them.

The scale of the operation, nearly 6,500 profiles across TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram, shows that platform moderation did not catch the content at the point of publication. It took a third-party anti-piracy firm, hired by the attorney himself, to identify and remove the profiles. The victims were directed off-platform to WhatsApp and then asked to pay through peer-to-peer apps that offer little recourse, which is a deliberate structural choice by the scammers to avoid recoverable transactions.

It is not established who is responsible for creating the content, no arrests or charges are reported, and the full financial harm to victims is not quantified in the available reporting.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become a victim of AI-powered scams targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using artificial intelligence to impersonate him and offer fraudulent immigration services. The scams direct people through social media to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, where scammers send fake contracts and request payments between $2,200 and unspecified amounts through apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App.

Leal first discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity began last October and escalated dramatically over the past three months. His firm hired an anti-piracy company that successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The fake videos falsely promise US residency assistance and include testimonials from supposed former clients. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams and urges immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to avoid payments through digital payment apps.
